source_metadata.title: A Randomized Trial of Intensive versus Standard Blood-Pressure Control
source_metadata.correction_note: 2017 correction changes two Framingham-risk baseline rows in Table 1; corrected values are used here.

atoms.canonical_statement: SPRINT tested whether targeting systolic blood pressure below 120 mm Hg would reduce cardiovascular events more than targeting below 140 mm Hg in high-risk adults without diabetes.
SPRINT was a randomized, controlled, open-label trial conducted at 102 clinical sites in the United States, including Puerto Rico; outcome adjudicators were blinded to treatment assignment.

Participants were required to be at least 50 years old, have systolic blood pressure 130-180 mm Hg, and have increased cardiovascular risk defined by established cardiovascular disease, CKD with eGFR 20 to <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, Framingham 10-year CVD risk >=15%, or age >=75 years; diabetes and prior stroke were excluded.
The intensive-treatment strategy targeted systolic blood pressure below 120 mm Hg, with monthly medication adjustment until target or a clinical decision not to intensify further.

exposures.details: Target systolic blood pressure <120 mm Hg; antihypertensive therapy titrated to target.

atoms.canonical_statement: The standard-treatment strategy targeted systolic blood pressure below 140 mm Hg, with step-down therapy when SBP was <130 mm Hg at one visit or <135 mm Hg on two consecutive protocol visits.

exposures.details: Target systolic blood pressure <140 mm Hg; standard-group medication reduction rules applied for lower SBP.

atoms.canonical_statement: Blood pressure was based on the mean of three seated measurements after 5 minutes of quiet rest using an automated Omron Model 907 system in the main trial; the protocol preferred automated measurement to reduce observer bias.
The primary outcome was the first occurrence of myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, heart failure, or death from cardiovascular causes.

outcome.definition: First occurrence of myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, heart failure, or cardiovascular death.

atoms.canonical_statement: The planned primary analysis used time-to-first-event methods under intention-to-treat; the target enrollment of 9250 provided an estimated 88.7% power to detect a 20% treatment effect assuming a 2.2%/year primary-event rate in the standard group.
The protocol specified group-sequential interim monitoring for efficacy and futility; the August 2015 interim boundary was crossed and the blood-pressure intervention was stopped early.
At 1 year, mean systolic blood pressure was 121.4 mm Hg with intensive treatment and 136.2 mm Hg with standard treatment, a 14.8 mm Hg between-group difference.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that an SBP target below 120 mm Hg, compared with below 140 mm Hg, reduced major cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in high-risk patients without diabetes, while increasing some adverse events.

atoms.canonical_statement: The trial did not establish generalizability to patients with diabetes, prior stroke, age under 50 years, or older adults residing in nursing homes or assisted-living facilities.
The blood-pressure intervention was stopped early after a median 3.26 years because the efficacy boundary was crossed, limiting the duration of randomized exposure and long-term safety assessment.

SPRINT was funded by the National Institutes of Health, including NHLBI with cosponsorship by NIDDK, NINDS, and NIA; azilsartan products were donated by Takeda and Arbor Pharmaceuticals, which otherwise had no role in the study.
